name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_Q01 - IUPAC name of vanillin structure

questiontext.text: Identify the correct IUPAC name of the naturally occurring flavouring compound whose structure is shown below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In IUPAC nomenclature of substituted aromatic aldehydes, the carbon atom of the benzene ring bearing the aldehyde group (\(-\mathrm{CHO}\)) is assigned position 1, and the ring is numbered to give the lowest locants to the remaining substituents, which are cited in alphabetical order.

Step 2: Structure Interpretation
The given structure (vanillin) consists of a benzene ring with an aldehyde group (\(-\mathrm{CHO}\)) at C-1, a methoxy group (\(-\mathrm{OCH_3}\)) at C-3, and a hydroxyl group (\(-\mathrm{OH}\)) at C-4.

Step 3: Applying Nomenclature Rules
Alphabetically, "hydroxy" comes before "methoxy". Combining the locants and prefixes with the parent name "benzaldehyde" yields 4-hydroxy-3-methoxybenzaldehyde.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct IUPAC name of the compound is 4-hydroxy-3-methoxybenzaldehyde.

answer.text: 3-Hydroxy-4-methoxybenzaldehyde
4-Hydroxy-3-methoxybenzaldehyde
2-Hydroxy-3-methoxybenzaldehyde
4-Methoxy-3-hydroxyacetophenone

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_Q02 - Hydrogen-bonded dimer of carboxylic acids

questiontext.text:
The diagram below represents a characteristic molecular association of carboxylic acids:

Which statement accurately describes this structure and its physical significance?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Carboxylic acids contain both a hydrogen-bond donor (\(-\mathrm{OH}\)) and a hydrogen-bond acceptor (\(\mathrm{C=O}\)) within the same carboxyl group, enabling strong intermolecular association.

Step 2: Diagram Interpretation
The diagram shows two carboxylic acid molecules (\(\mathrm{RCOOH}\)) linked by two intermolecular hydrogen bonds between the carbonyl oxygen of one molecule and the hydroxyl hydrogen of the other, forming a stable eight-membered cyclic dimer.

Step 3: Physical Significance
These hydrogen bonds are so strong that they are not broken completely even in the vapour phase or in aprotic solvents. This extensive association explains why carboxylic acids have higher boiling points than aldehydes, ketones, and even alcohols of comparable molecular masses.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The structure represents an intermolecular hydrogen-bonded dimer of carboxylic acids that exists in the vapour state or in aprotic solvents.

answer.text: Ionic salt bridge formed by carboxylic acids in aqueous alkali
Covalent anhydride formed on heating carboxylic acids with phosphorus pentoxide
Intramolecular hydrogen bonding in dicarboxylic acids in aqueous solution
Intermolecular hydrogen-bonded dimer of carboxylic acids in the vapour state or aprotic solvents

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_Q03 - Orbital diagram of the carbonyl group

questiontext.text:
The orbital diagram for the formation of a carbonyl group is shown below:

Which of the following statements correctly describes the bonding and geometry depicted in the diagram?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The carbonyl carbon atom forms three \(\sigma\)-bonds and one \(\pi\)-bond, which determines its hybridisation state and spatial geometry.

Step 2: Diagram Interpretation
The diagram shows that the carbonyl carbon is \(sp^2\)-hybridised and forms three \(\sigma\)-bonds (one with oxygen and two with attached substituents) lying in a single plane with bond angles of approximately \(120^\circ\).

Step 3: \(\pi\)-Bond Formation
The fourth valence electron of carbon occupies an unhybridised \(p\)-orbital perpendicular to the molecular plane and overlaps sideways with a \(p\)-orbital of the oxygen atom to form a \(\pi\)-bond, placing the \(\pi\)-electron cloud above and below the trigonal coplanar framework.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The carbonyl carbon is \(sp^2\)-hybridised with trigonal coplanar geometry (\(120^\circ\) bond angles), and the \(\pi\)-bond is formed by sideways overlap of unhybridised \(p\)-orbitals of carbon and oxygen.

answer.text: The carbonyl carbon is \(sp^2\)-hybridised with trigonal coplanar geometry (\(\sim 120^\circ\) bond angles), and the \(\pi\)-bond is formed by sideways overlap of unhybridised \(p\)-orbitals of carbon and oxygen.
The carbonyl carbon is \(sp^3\)-hybridised with tetrahedral geometry (\(\sim 109.5^\circ\) bond angles), and the \(\pi\)-bond is formed by head-on overlap of \(sp^2\) orbitals.
The carbonyl carbon is \(sp\)-hybridised with linear geometry (\(180^\circ\) bond angle), and the oxygen atom has no non-bonding electron pairs.
The carbonyl carbon is \(sp^2\)-hybridised, and all three \(\sigma\)-bonds along with the \(\pi\)-electron cloud lie strictly within the same plane.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_Q04 - Mechanism of nucleophilic addition to carbonyls

questiontext.text:
The mechanism of nucleophilic attack on a carbonyl carbon is illustrated below:

Which statement correctly describes the hybridisation change and rate-determining step shown in this mechanism?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Aldehydes and ketones undergo nucleophilic addition because the carbonyl carbon is electrophilic (\(\delta^+\)) due to the higher electronegativity of oxygen.

Step 2: Diagram Interpretation
In the slow (rate-determining) step, the nucleophile (\(\mathrm{Nu^-}\)) attacks the planar, \(sp^2\)-hybridised carbonyl carbon from a direction approximately perpendicular to the plane of the \(sp^2\) orbitals.

Step 3: Hybridisation and Intermediate
As the \(\mathrm{C-Nu}\) bond forms and the \(\pi\)-electron pair shifts onto oxygen, the hybridisation of the carbonyl carbon changes from \(sp^2\) to \(sp^3\), generating a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate. This intermediate subsequently captures a proton (\(\mathrm{H^+}\)) from the reaction medium to yield the neutral addition product.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The carbonyl carbon changes from \(sp^2\) to \(sp^3\) hybridisation to form a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate in the slow step.

answer.text: The carbonyl carbon changes from \(sp^3\) to \(sp^2\), and protonation of the alkoxide ion is the slow step.
The nucleophile attacks in the plane of the carbonyl group, and the resulting intermediate is trigonal planar.
The carbonyl carbon changes from \(sp^2\) to \(sp^3\) to form a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate in the slow step.
The nucleophile displaces the carbonyl oxygen in a single concerted step without forming an intermediate.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_Q05 - Resonance in benzaldehyde and nucleophilic reactivity

questiontext.text:
Consider the resonance interaction shown below for benzaldehyde:

How does this resonance effect influence the reactivity of benzaldehyde compared to propanal towards nucleophilic addition reactions?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The rate of nucleophilic addition to a carbonyl compound increases with the electrophilicity (partial positive charge) of the carbonyl carbon.

Step 2: Diagram Interpretation
The curved arrows in the diagram show \(\pi\)-electron density shifting from the benzene ring towards the carbonyl group, creating a double bond between the ring and the carbonyl carbon while placing a negative charge on the carbonyl oxygen and a positive charge on the aromatic ring.

Step 3: Reactivity Comparison
This resonance delocalisation reduces the polarity and electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon in benzaldehyde relative to an aliphatic aldehyde such as propanal, where no such resonance donation exists. Consequently, benzaldehyde is less reactive than propanal towards nucleophilic addition.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Resonance reduces the polarity and electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon, making benzaldehyde less reactive than propanal.

answer.text: Resonance increases the positive charge on the carbonyl carbon, making benzaldehyde more reactive than propanal.
Resonance reduces the polarity and electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon, making benzaldehyde less reactive than propanal.
Resonance converts the carbonyl carbon into an \(sp^3\)-hybridised centre, completely preventing nucleophilic attack.
Resonance makes the benzene ring strongly electron-rich, directing nucleophiles to the ortho and para positions.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_Q06 - Acidity of alpha-hydrogens and enolate stabilisation

questiontext.text:
The chemical process depicted below involves abstraction of a proton by a base (\(\mathrm{:B}\)):

Which important chemical behaviour of aldehydes and ketones is directly explained by this process?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Carbonyl compounds possessing at least one \(\alpha\)-hydrogen atom exhibit characteristic reactivity in basic media due to the acidity of the \(\alpha\)-proton.

Step 2: Diagram Interpretation
The diagram shows a base (\(\mathrm{:B}\)) removing an \(\alpha\)-hydrogen from the carbon adjacent to the carbonyl group. The resulting carbanion is stabilised by resonance with the carbonyl group, delocalising the negative charge onto the electronegative oxygen atom (forming an enolate ion).

Step 3: Reaction Outcome
Because of the strong electron-withdrawing effect of the carbonyl group and resonance stabilisation of the conjugate base, \(\alpha\)-hydrogens are acidic, enabling aldehydes and ketones to undergo aldol condensation in the presence of dilute alkali.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The process explains the acidity of \(\alpha\)-hydrogen atoms, which enables aldol reactions in dilute alkali.

answer.text: Higher boiling points of ketones compared to ethers of comparable molecular mass
Oxidation of aliphatic aldehydes by Tollens' reagent to form a silver mirror
Acid-catalysed addition of alcohols to aldehydes to yield acetals
Acidity of \(\alpha\)-hydrogen atoms enabling aldol reactions in the presence of dilute alkali

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_Q07 - Conversion of phthalic acid to phthalimide

questiontext.text:
In the reaction sequence shown below, phthalic acid reacts with ammonia to form ammonium phthalate, which upon heating yields phthalamide and finally phthalimide:

Which small molecule is eliminated during the final strong-heating step that converts phthalamide into cyclic phthalimide?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Carboxylic acids react with ammonia to form ammonium salts, which lose water upon heating to produce amides. Ortho-dicarboxylic acids can undergo further cyclisation upon strong heating.

Step 2: Diagram Interpretation
In the first step, phthalic acid reacts with \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) to form ammonium phthalate. Heating this salt eliminates two molecules of water (\(-2\mathrm{H_2O}\)) to give phthalamide, which has two \(-\mathrm{CONH_2}\) groups at adjacent positions.

Step 3: Final Cyclisation Step
On strong heating, the two adjacent amide groups in phthalamide undergo intramolecular cyclisation with the elimination of one molecule of ammonia (\(-\mathrm{NH_3}\)) to yield the five-membered cyclic imide, phthalimide.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Ammonia (\(\mathrm{NH_3}\)) is eliminated in the final strong-heating step.

answer.text: Ammonia (\(\mathrm{NH_3}\))
Water (\(\mathrm{H_2O}\))
Carbon dioxide (\(\mathrm{CO_2}\))
Nitrogen (\(\mathrm{N_2}\))

questiontext.text:
The mechanism for the acid-catalysed esterification of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol is shown below:

Which statement accurately describes the key mechanistic events illustrated in this scheme?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Acid-catalysed esterification of carboxylic acids with alcohols proceeds via a nucleophilic acyl substitution mechanism.

Step 2: Activation and Nucleophilic Attack
First, protonation of the carbonyl oxygen by \(\mathrm{H^+}\) increases the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon, activating it towards nucleophilic addition by the weakly nucleophilic alcohol (\(\mathrm{R'OH}\)) to form a tetrahedral intermediate.

Step 3: Proton Transfer and Elimination
Proton transfer within the tetrahedral intermediate converts one of the hydroxyl (\(-\mathrm{OH}\)) groups into a better leaving group (\(-\mathrm{OH_2^+}\)), which is then eliminated as a neutral water molecule (\(-\mathrm{HOH}\)). Finally, deprotonation of the protonated ester yields the neutral ester.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Protonation of the carbonyl oxygen activates the carbonyl group towards nucleophilic attack by the alcohol, and proton transfer converts \(-\mathrm{OH}\) into \(-\mathrm{OH_2^+}\), which leaves as a neutral water molecule.

answer.text: The acid catalyst deprotonates the alcohol to form an alkoxide ion, and a hydroxide ion (\(\mathrm{OH^-}\)) is eliminated as the leaving group.
Protonation occurs at the hydroxyl oxygen of the carboxylic acid, and the alcohol is eliminated without forming a tetrahedral intermediate.

Protonation of the carbonyl oxygen activates the carbonyl group toward nucleophilic attack by the alcohol, and proton transfer converts \(-\mathrm{OH}\) into \(-\mathrm{OH_2^+}\), which leaves as a neutral water molecule.
The ester bond is formed by direct \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) displacement of the carboxyl hydroxyl group by the alcohol in a single step.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_Q09 - Chemoselective reduction with sodium borohydride

questiontext.text: Predict the major organic product of the reaction shown below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Sodium borohydride (\(\mathrm{NaBH_4}\)) is a mild, chemoselective reducing agent that reduces aldehydes and ketones to alcohols, but does not reduce carboxylic acids or esters under normal conditions.

Step 2: Substrate Analysis
The starting compound, \(\mathrm{CH_3COCH_2COOC_2H_5}\) (ethyl 3-oxobutanoate), contains both a ketone carbonyl group at C-3 and an ester functional group at C-1.

Step 3: Applying Reagent Selectivity
On treatment with \(\mathrm{NaBH_4}\) followed by acidic work-up (\(\mathrm{H^+}\)), only the ketonic carbonyl group is reduced to a secondary alcohol (\(-\mathrm{CH(OH)}-\)), while the ester group (\(-\mathrm{COOC_2H_5}\)) remains intact. This gives \(\mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CH_2COOC_2H_5}\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The major organic product is ethyl 3-hydroxybutanoate.

answer.text: Butane-1,3-diol
Ethyl 3-hydroxybutanoate
3-Hydroxybutanoic acid
Ethyl butanoate

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_Q10 - Reductive ozonolysis yielding two cyclohexanone molecules

questiontext.text: Identify the starting alkene in the reductive ozonolysis reaction shown below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Reductive ozonolysis of an alkene (\(\mathrm{O_3}\) followed by \(\mathrm{Zn/H_2O}\)) cleaves the \(\mathrm{C=C}\) double bond completely and replaces the double-bonded carbons with carbonyl (\(\mathrm{C=O}\)) oxygens.

Step 2: Retrosynthetic Analysis
The product consists of two identical molecules of cyclohexanone. Removing the two carbonyl oxygen atoms from the two cyclohexanone molecules and joining their carbonyl carbons directly with a \(\mathrm{C=C}\) double bond reconstructs the parent alkene.

Step 3: Evaluating Alternatives
Cyclohexene upon ozonolysis would give hexane-1,6-dial, whereas methylenecyclohexane would give one molecule of cyclohexanone and one molecule of methanal. Only two cyclohexane rings joined by an exocyclic double bond between C-1 and C-1' (cyclohexylidenecyclohexane) cleave to give two molecules of cyclohexanone.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The starting alkene is cyclohexylidenecyclohexane.

answer.text: Cyclohexene
1-Methylcyclohexene
Methylenecyclohexane
Cyclohexylidenecyclohexane
